entities.name: Gnaeus Acerronius Proculus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gnaeus Acerronius Proculus served as one of the two ordinary consuls of the Roman Empire in 37 AD, sharing the highest magistracy with his colleague Gaius Petronius Pontius Nigrinus. His consulship, while not marked by extraordinary personal achievements, holds a distinct place in Roman imperial history as it coincided with the pivotal death of Emperor Tiberius and the subsequent accession of Gaius Caesar, famously known as Caligula. As a member of the senatorial elite, his elevation to the consulship signifies the continued functioning of the Roman administrative and political system even amidst the profound shifts in imperial power, reflecting the established cursus honorum for ambitious Roman aristocrats.

During his six-month tenure as consul, from January 1 to June 30, 37 AD, Acerronius Proculus presided over the Roman Senate and the formal commencement of the Roman year, a period of immense political tension and uncertainty. The death of Tiberius on March 16, 37 AD, at Misenum, transformed his consulship from a routine administrative role into a witness to imperial transition. The consuls were instrumental in the constitutional formalities surrounding the transfer of power, including the recognition of Tiberius’ will, the Senate’s acclamation of Caligula, and the subsequent deification of Tiberius, all of which unfolded under their nominal authority. His name, alongside Nigrinus, appears in the *Fasti Capitolini* and other epigraphic evidence, marking the year in official records.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gnaeus Acerronius Proculus's consulship in 37 AD is historically significant not for his personal actions, but because it coincided with the death of Emperor Tiberius and the accession of Caligula, symbolizing the continuity of Roman state institutions during a critical imperial transition.
